title: Pregnancy and postpartum stroke
summary: Pregnancy-associated stroke has diverse mechanisms and requires coordinated neurovascular and obstetric care. The 2026 AHA statement addresses urgent evaluation, prevention, maternal stabilization and recovery needs extending into the postpartum period.
consider: Have the pregnancy or postpartum stage, blood pressure and likely stroke mechanism been established?
Are vascular neurology and maternal-fetal medicine involved in timely imaging and treatment decisions?
Does the recovery plan address infant care, breastfeeding and rehabilitation support?
caution: Pregnancy alone should not delay stroke evaluation. This statement does not make acute stroke an automatic indication for delivery or supply a universal antithrombotic choice.

title: Stroke with active cancer
summary: Active cancer can coexist with conventional stroke mechanisms or contribute directly to thrombosis. The 2026 AHA statement proposes graded certainty for cancer-related causation and emphasizes substantial remaining treatment uncertainty.
consider: Has the usual arterial and cardiac evaluation been completed rather than attributing the event to cancer alone?
What clinical evidence supports cancer-related thrombosis or another cancer-associated mechanism?
Have recurrent thrombosis, bleeding, cancer treatment and patient goals been reviewed together?
caution: A cancer diagnosis does not establish the stroke mechanism or an automatic anticoagulant indication. Treatment evidence varies by mechanism and population.

title: Stroke with prior disability or dementia
summary: Patients with prior disability or dementia were commonly excluded from reperfusion trials. Observational evidence supports considering the possibility of returning to the person’s own baseline within individualized, transparent decisions.
consider: What were the patient’s actual baseline function, supports and valued activities?
What additional disability might this stroke cause, and what outcome would the patient consider worthwhile?
Are treatment risks and the limits of the evidence being discussed without relying on a baseline score alone?
caution: Prior disability is not a complete treatment decision. Observational findings do not establish benefit for every patient; prognosis and goals require individual review.

title: Perioperative stroke
summary: Perioperative stroke care spans preoperative risk assessment, coordinated hemodynamic and medication planning, and rapid recognition of new postoperative deficits. The AHA statement concerns noncardiac, nonneurological surgery.
consider: Are recent stroke history, vascular disease and the proposed procedure included in the risk discussion?
Are perioperative medication changes and the responsible teams clearly documented?
Does a new postoperative deficit trigger the local stroke pathway with prompt imaging?
caution: Timing after a recent stroke and perioperative medication changes require current guidance, procedure-specific bleeding assessment and multidisciplinary review; this card does not supply a universal surgery date.

title: Sex, gender and equitable stroke care
summary: The AHA statement examines sex- and gender-related differences in endovascular care and the effects of social and cultural context. Much of the available literature records sex rather than gender, leaving important knowledge gaps.
consider: Could differences in recognition, access, baseline circumstances or support be influencing care?
Are decisions based on the individual’s clinical findings and priorities?
Does the cited evidence actually address this patient population?
caution: Population-level differences do not establish an individual treatment effect or a separate automatic eligibility rule.

title: Stroke in neonates and children
summary: The AHA pediatric statement distinguishes perinatal from later childhood stroke and reviews age-specific presentation, mechanisms, evaluation and recovery. Childhood stroke can be difficult to recognize and may present with seizures or less-localizing symptoms.
consider: Does the presentation warrant urgent pediatric stroke expertise and age-appropriate imaging?
Have age-specific mechanisms and stroke mimics been considered?
Does follow-up address development, learning, family support and recurrence prevention?
caution: Adult pathways cannot simply be transferred to neonates or children. The 2019 statement predates the 2026 AIS guideline; acute reperfusion decisions need current pediatric expertise.

title: Sickle cell cerebrovascular disease
summary: ASH guidance addresses overt stroke, silent cerebral injury and prevention in children and adults with sickle cell disease. Its cerebrovascular recommendations require disease-specific hematology and neurology coordination.
consider: Are the sickle cell genotype, prior cerebral events and preventive treatment history known?
Has a new neurologic event prompted urgent stroke and hematology assessment?
Is the age- and disease-specific screening and follow-up plan clear?
caution: An adult atherosclerotic-stroke pathway does not cover sickle cell disease. Transfusion and disease-modifying decisions require the full guideline and the treating specialists.

title: Dysphagia, nutrition and oral care
summary: ESO/ESSD guidance supports systematic dysphagia screening and assessment when risk is identified. Swallowing care connects aspiration prevention with nutrition, hydration, oral health and individualized rehabilitation.
consider: Is swallowing safety assessed and the current intake plan communicated to the team?
Does a concerning screen or clinical change require specialist assessment?
Are nutrition, hydration, oral care and reassessment included in the plan?
caution: A screening result does not determine the full swallowing diagnosis. Evidence quality differs across interventions; texture, feeding and rehabilitation decisions need individualized review.

title: Stroke-associated pneumonia
summary: The 2026 ESO guideline addresses pneumonia diagnosis, prevention and treatment after stroke. It favors consistent diagnostic assessment and individualized prevention; preventive antibiotics have not improved relevant outcomes.
consider: Is pneumonia supported by a clinical assessment rather than a risk score alone?
Have swallowing, positioning, mobility and nutritional needs been reviewed?
If pneumonia is diagnosed, is treatment aligned with local microbiology and antimicrobial guidance?
caution: Most questions in this guideline rely on expert consensus because direct evidence is limited. A prediction score does not diagnose pneumonia or justify prophylactic antibiotics.

title: Stroke-unit nursing and daily care
summary: AHA nursing statements describe interprofessional care across the hyperacute, postinterventional and ward phases. The posthyperacute statement connects consistent inpatient care with patient and family preparation for discharge.
consider: Are phase-specific monitoring and escalation responsibilities clear?
Have functional needs, safety concerns and family teaching been incorporated into daily care?
Are unresolved inpatient issues carried forward into the discharge plan?
caution: These statements complement current acute stroke guidance and local nursing procedures. They do not supply a universal monitoring frequency or replace a response to clinical deterioration.

title: Systemic complications during stroke admission
summary: Nonneurological complications affect multiple organ systems after ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. The AHA statement emphasizes coordinated surveillance and management while acknowledging gaps in the evidence.
consider: Have new systemic symptoms or laboratory changes been assessed alongside the neurologic course?
Could language impairment be limiting the examination, and does fluctuating attention require broader reassessment?
Are medical, nursing and rehabilitation teams sharing an explicit complication-management plan?
caution: Aphasia, delirium and neurologic deterioration may coexist. A bedside impression or reference card cannot exclude an acute cause of change; management depends on the identified complication.

title: VTE prevention after stroke
summary: In immobile patients with ischemic stroke, ESO guidance supports intermittent pneumatic compression. Pharmacologic prophylaxis requires balancing thromboembolic benefit against intracranial and extracranial bleeding risks.
consider: What are the current mobility, VTE and bleeding risks?
Is the chosen mechanical method appropriate and being used as intended?
If medication prophylaxis is considered, have renal function, recent treatment and hemorrhage risk been reviewed?
caution: The source concerns immobile ischemic-stroke patients. ICH and postprocedure decisions need their own guidance; graduated compression stockings are not equivalent to intermittent pneumatic compression.

title: Spasticity and contracture prevention
summary: Poststroke spasticity can combine involuntary muscle activity, impaired voluntary control and tissue changes. The 2026 AHA statement emphasizes earlier recognition and access to care before secondary impairment becomes established.
consider: Are pain, hygiene, positioning, mobility or care tasks affected by tone or restricted movement?
What active and passive functional goals matter to the patient and caregiver?
Is timely specialist or rehabilitation assessment needed?
caution: Increased tone is not the only cause of impaired movement. Treatment choice should follow a functional assessment; this card does not select a drug, injection pattern or procedure.

title: Aphasia and communication rehabilitation
summary: ESO guidance supports individualized speech-language therapy and evaluates therapy amount, delivery and meaningful communication outcomes. Digital and group formats can be considered within an appropriate rehabilitation plan.
consider: Which communication activities matter most to the patient?
Are assessment and shared decisions adapted to language impairment?
Is the therapy plan feasible, sufficiently supported and reassessed as needs change?
caution: Evidence certainty differs across therapy comparisons. Aphasia does not establish impaired decision-making capacity, and communication difficulty should not be assumed to explain every cognitive or behavioral change.

title: Visual impairment and neglect
summary: ESO guidance addresses detection and assessment of poststroke visual problems across central vision, eye movements, visual fields, neglect and perception. Screening can identify needs that are otherwise missed.
consider: Has the patient been assessed for the relevant type of visual impairment?
Do reading, mobility or daily activities require adaptations and specialist input?
Are visual findings communicated to the rehabilitation and follow-up teams?
caution: Different visual syndromes require different assessments; evidence for treatment varies. This card does not establish driving fitness or substitute for specialist visual evaluation.

title: Motor recovery, walking and daily activity
summary: ESO motor-rehabilitation guidance reviews upper-limb practice, gait training, therapy transfer into daily life, group therapy and sit-to-stand training. Recommendations differ in strength and in the population studied.
consider: Which movement and participation goals are being measured over time?
Is practice linked to tasks the patient needs in daily life?
Do cardiovascular stability, endurance and access support the proposed training approach?
caution: A finding in chronic, cardiovascularly stable stroke does not automatically apply during acute illness. Therapy dose and intensity need a rehabilitation assessment rather than a universal schedule.

title: Mood, anxiety, fatigue and psychosocial recovery
summary: The AHA psychosocial statement considers depression, stress, anxiety, fatigue and quality of life after stroke. It emphasizes recognition, appropriate screening, education and access to interdisciplinary support.
consider: Which emotional symptoms or fatigue are limiting recovery or daily life?
Is a concerning screen followed by clinical assessment and a practical care pathway?
Do the patient and family have support, education and access to needed services?
caution: A screening score is not a diagnosis. Evidence for specific nursing interventions is limited, and fatigue or distress should not be assigned a single cause without assessment.

title: Driving, seizures and return to participation
summary: The AAN seizure-driving position statement supports individualized licensing assessment and addresses medication effects, seizure recurrence and access to alternative transportation. Driving and other participation goals should be discussed explicitly during follow-up.
consider: Are seizures, cognition, vision, motor function or medication effects relevant to the intended activity?
Have the applicable licensing rules and any specialist assessment requirements been checked?
What transport, workplace or rehabilitation support is needed?
caution: An AAN consensus position is not state law, a universal poststroke waiting period or individual clearance. Driving rules and occupational demands require separate review.

title: Long-term follow-up and primary care
summary: AHA primary-care guidance combines recurrent-stroke prevention with function, late complications and quality of life. Screening for cognition, mood, falls and unmet needs remains relevant beyond the early recovery period.
consider: Are risk-factor treatment and the medication list reconciled across clinicians?
Have changes in function, falls, cognition or mood prompted reassessment?
Are patient and caregiver priorities linked to referrals and a named follow-up plan?
caution: A stable initial follow-up does not resolve future recovery needs. Prevention and rehabilitation plans require reassessment as health, function and support change.

title: Cognition after stroke and vascular brain injury
summary: Cognitive impairment after stroke can affect independence, employment and relationships. Vascular injury and preexisting neurodegenerative disease may interact; screening for associated conditions and interdisciplinary management are important.
consider: What has changed from the person’s cognitive and functional baseline?
Are language, mood, sensory limitations or acute illness affecting assessment?
Does the care plan address everyday safety, supports and follow-up evaluation?
caution: A single screen does not identify the full cause or establish permanent impairment. Early cognitive changes can evolve; review the trajectory and possible contributing conditions.

title: Sleep disorders and brain health
summary: The AHA statement links disturbed sleep and sleep disorders with adverse cerebrovascular and cognitive outcomes. These associations support identifying sleep concerns, while causal pathways and treatment effects remain incompletely established.
consider: Are sleep-disordered breathing, insomnia or other sleep symptoms affecting recovery?
Does screening warrant diagnostic evaluation rather than an assumed diagnosis?
Are sleep symptoms and treatment feasibility included in follow-up?
caution: An association with stroke or dementia does not prove that a particular sleep intervention prevents either outcome. A screening questionnaire does not diagnose sleep apnea.

title: Brain health across the life span
summary: The 2026 AHA framework places brain health within lifelong physical, emotional, environmental and social influences. It reviews potential mechanisms and prevention opportunities while distinguishing established knowledge from research questions.
consider: Which vascular, sleep, mental-health or social factors are relevant to this person’s goals?
Are potentially modifiable exposures and barriers discussed without overinterpreting observational findings?
Does the proposed intervention have evidence for the outcome being claimed?
caution: This framework is a scientific statement for future study, not a validated brain-health score or proof that a supplement, biomarker or lifestyle intervention prevents dementia.

title: Antiamyloid therapy and cerebrovascular risk
summary: Antiamyloid immunotherapies can cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, including edema and hemorrhage. The AHA advisory examines questions involving cerebrovascular disease, antithrombotics and acute stroke presentations in treated patients.
consider: Is current or recent antiamyloid treatment known and communicated to the stroke team?
Could the presentation and imaging reflect ARIA, ischemia or another process?
Have the current drug label, imaging history and relevant specialists been consulted?
caution: The advisory highlights important evidence gaps. This card supplies no blanket antithrombotic or reperfusion permission; acute decisions require current drug-specific and stroke guidance.

title: In-hospital stroke recognition and response
summary: The AHA statement identifies staff recognition, rapid access to stroke expertise, standardized assessment and imaging, transfer planning and quality feedback as core elements of an in-hospital stroke system.
consider: Can staff immediately activate the stroke response from this location?
Are timing, examination, imaging and relevant recent procedures communicated to the response team?
Are transfer barriers and delays captured for review?
caution: Being in a monitored setting does not ensure timely recognition. A systems statement complements current treatment guidance and the institution’s stroke pathway.

title: Rural care, telestroke and transfer networks
summary: AHA statements emphasize dependable access to expertise, clear transfer processes and collaboration between lower-resourced hospitals and larger stroke centers. Virtual networks can improve coordination when their clinical and operational limits are understood.
consider: What imaging, specialist and treatment capabilities are available at the referring and receiving sites?
Are clinical information, images and the transfer plan shared through a reliable process?
Is responsibility clear if connection, transport or destination capacity changes?
caution: Technology and center labels do not establish current local capability. Routing and treatment require the actual clinical assessment, regional agreements and available resources.

title: Transitions, discharge communication and continuity
summary: The AHA transitions statement emphasizes matching care with patient preferences, coordination, education, comfort, emotional support, family involvement and continuity. These domains are not consistently represented in studied transition interventions.
consider: Are the patient’s priorities and support needs reflected in the next setting of care?
Are medication plans, outstanding questions and responsibility for follow-up clearly communicated?
Have the patient and care partner received usable information and a way to seek help?
caution: A completed discharge document does not establish a successful transition. Understanding, access and follow-through need direct confirmation.

title: Rehabilitation access and recovery barriers
summary: AHA statements identify insurance processes, geography and social or environmental conditions as barriers to rehabilitation and recovery. A workable plan must connect clinical needs with realistic access to services.
consider: Do coverage, travel, caregiving or other circumstances limit the proposed rehabilitation plan?
Are the recommended setting and services linked to documented functional needs?
Who will help resolve barriers and reassess needs if access is delayed?
caution: Placement availability is not the same as clinical suitability. Broad policy recommendations do not predict an individual insurer’s decision or replace reassessment of the patient’s needs.

Are processes and outcomes measured with clear responsibility for improvement?
